utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody, both in the courtroom and those assisting us from just outside the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. In view of the next witness to be called by the Prosecution, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will immediately rule on the oral application for protective measures, the standard being an objectively grounded risk to security or the welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness has given evidence before this Tribunal. We have two different ways to meet that standard, since the second three-prong test has been met, there's no need to further consider the factual basis for the threats which are under the first test. The second three-prong test being that combination of the following: That the witness's testimony may antagonise persons who reside in, in this case, in the former Yugoslavia, in Kosovo; that the family of the witness live in that territory; and that there is -- exists an unstable security situation in the territory which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. And as it appears from pages 3955 and 56, the parties have agreed upon the -- on the fulfilment of this last condition; therefore, the protective measures are granted. Mr. Registrar, since the reasons for the protective measures have to be delivered in open session, the last few words can be made public on the transcript, because we're still in -- we are still in private session. The protective measures, face distortion -- distortion -- voice distortion, and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now turn into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber just granted protective measures for the next witness to be called; the relevant portion of the transcript, which is now still in private session, can be made public. That is, only the reasons for granting these protective measures. Now, for the witness to enter the courtroom, we have to pull the curtains down. I do understand that all preparations are put in place for face distortion and voice distortion; the pseudonym of the witness will be Witness 52. Meanwhile, I perhaps already could address a few matters. There is a Prosecution motion, a combined motion for the testimony of -- under 92 bis or to subpoena the relevant witness. That was a motion filed on the 17th of October. And the Chamber would very much like to receive the response by the Defence as soon as possible. That is, this week. Then -- yes. Similarly, the Chamber would very much like to receive a response to the Prosecution's ninth motion for the testimony via videolink, a motion for which an addendum was filed on the 19th of October in which but a legible and fully translated versions of the medical reports and the certificates are given. That are already two practical matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 52, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to stand. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I usually invite witnesses to read that statement, to make that statement by reading the text. Can you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I must read, yes, I can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Madam Usher will hand out to you now the text of the solemn declaration and I'll read it first for you. It says: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." Would you please make that solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness 52. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Curtains can be drawn up again. Witness 52, I do not address you by your own name because the Trial Chamber has decided that you will testify with a pseudonym, that is, not using your name but calling you "Witness 52"; and also, that your face will not be broadcasted and your voice also will be distorted so that although the outside world can hear the content of your testimony, they can't see your face, they can't hear your own voice. You will first be examined by Mr. Di Fazio, who's counsel for the Prosecution. He's standing over there, so perhaps you look at him. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to look at the television screen that's in front of you because I'm going to ask that a document be put up on it. And you can just have a look at it. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 2101, please. Now, that's got some English and some of your own language in writing there. Can you look at those details and can you tell us if those details are correct; namely, your last name, your first name, (redacted) first name, your date of birth, and your place of birth. Are they -- are they correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll add the allocation of the numbers to Professor Aleksandric's exhibits. This would be P1137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, and under seal. No objections. Therefore, admitted into evidence. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more personal detail that I need to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- is it -- can that be done -- MR. DI FAZIO: We're still in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're in open session at this point. MR. DI FAZIO: My apologies. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until now you just said what kind of data -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there was on the pseudonym sheet but not any detail. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then turn into private session. MR. DI FAZIO: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us if in the mid-part of 1998 (redacted) was still carrying out his occupation or whether he was retired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: He had retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that for health reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: He was ill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he residing in -- at home with you in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about -- thinking back to the time that you last saw (redacted), about how long before that would you say that he had retired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: A year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did (redacted) speak Serbian? I mean by that was he able to? Did he have a command of that language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to turn your mind, please, if you would, to the period of time around July of 1998. At that time, were you still residing in your village, in the village that -- whose name you mentioned in private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your family happy to be living in that village at that time, or did it take decisions about -- about leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: At that time, in July, we wanted to stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that in fact what you did, what your family did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever a time when you wanted to leave or tried to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember approximately when that was? If you can't remember, just say so; but if you can remember, tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: It was end of June, I think, or maybe the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- what happened at the end of June or maybe the beginning of July? Tell us in your own words what -- what -- what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't know what was going on and we heard that the police, the Serbian police, were leaving. The whole village was leaving. In fact, it was not like that. It was only the police that -- the Serbian police that were leaving. And we started to leave our village and some people told us, "You can go back to your home, because Albanians are not leaving. It's only the Serbs that are leaving," because the Serbs had been stationed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- I just want to ask you, to get a few more details about that answer that you just gave us. You -- you said that the Serbian police were leaving.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they leaving? How did you -- did you see anything or hear anything that indicated that the Serbian police were leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear where they were leaving from? Where were they leaving from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) But now you've told us that the police were leaving that village, and did that have any effect on -- on your family and on (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: We thought that the whole village were leaving, but -- well, I don't know. We went back home, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. But let me -- tell me if this -- if I understand you correctly. You -- your family actually left your own village but returned after being told that it was only the Serbian police that were leaving. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: We set off. We were trying to leave. We went halfway, and that's where we were told that, "You don't need to leave. It's only the Serbian police that are leaving and not the villagers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And can you tell the Trial Chamber, can you tell the Judges if -- if it was just your family alone that was -- was leaving or whether it was lots of families from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: There were other families as well. It was not only us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And they were also told the same thing, that they could go back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes, they returned as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who -- think back and do your best, but who explained to -- to the families, to your family and the other families that were leaving your village, that they could go back to their village? Who actually said that to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Well, when things are said in the village, you get to learn about them very soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you the question again. I'll try and be a little clearer. Okay? You've told us that you, your family, left the village and so did other families. But along the way, you told us --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along the way you told us that these families, including your family, were told that they could go back and only the Serbian police were leaving. Now, who told the family -- the families that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, yes, the second or the third time now that you said "only the Serb police was leaving" there. The witness testified that the -- not the Albanians were leaving but the Serbs were leaving. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not specifically Serb police which -- MR. DI FAZIO: I see. I don't want to compound my error and I'm grateful to Your Honours for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Witness 52 what Mr. Di Fazio very much would like to know, I take it, is that when you were told that you could go back, who exactly told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were a couple of young men and they said to us that we could go back because only the police are leaving -- leaving. And that was on the same day that we had set off. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember if these -- these young men were in uniform or had any insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: They were dressed normally, the ones that told us we could go back. They had their everyday clothes on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us if, in addition to being dressed in their everyday clothes, whether they were armed or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just may have missed asking you this: Why did you and your family want to leave? Do you know what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: The reason was (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps we should go into private session here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I jumped the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how long before (redacted) disappearance did -- would you say you saw these -- the last time you saw (redacted), anyway -- would you say that you saw these three men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Would you like me to give you a date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can. But, of course, if you can't give us a date, that's okay. But you just tell us if -- if it was a matter of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was the 1st of August. It was 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is this the same day that you last saw your (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw the group of three men on the last day that you saw (redacted).

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you received any other visits from those men before this one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did (redacted) own a weapon in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever give that weapon to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom -- you don't -- you don't have to use names, but to whom did he give his weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Unknown persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that on this very same day that he -- you last saw him, or did he give his weapon to unknown persons before, before that last day that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: It was on the day when we left the village and then returned. That was the day when these persons came and asked for the gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So let's talk about this day. Okay? Don't be nervous. It's -- you're -- just think about the questions and answer them. Now, we're talking about this day. And -- and you've told us that these three persons came and asked for the gun. Now, apart from the gun, did (redacted) give them anything -- anything else, apart from the gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: It was not a rifle. It was a pistol that he had a licence for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And he -- you've told us that he gave them that weapon. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- did (redacted) continue to reside in the house after this occasion when he handed over those items?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any more visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the last time you ever saw (redacted), when was the next visit? Or was it, in fact, on that occasion, the -- the last day you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Before (redacted) disappeared, two days earlier than that two people came. They searched the house and they couldn't find anything. And they came two days later then and took (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us a bit more about this visit where the house was searched. Firstly, did you know the -- the names or identities of the persons? And just indicate with a "yes" or a "no" and don't tell us the names, if you know them; but did you know the names, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No, that day, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So now I just want you to tell us more details of these -- of these people whose names you did not know and who came and searched your house. Were they -- how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: The last day they came and asked for (redacted) was sleeping at the time because he had had a heart attack, so he was taking medicine for that. Three people came and asked for him. We did not know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you there. We'll get on to this, but, first of all, I want to know about the occasion when two people came and searched the house before, before (redacted) disappeared. Okay? Now, let's just stick your mind -- keep your mind on that episode. All right? That's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm -- that's the episode I'm asking you about now. Now, on this day when the two people whose name you did not know came to the house, can you remember how they were dressed? These two people whose names you did not know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: They were -- they were in uniform, black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot say. But they had big jackets on and we did not have time to look properly. But they searched us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. They -- they searched the house, you've told us. And did -- did you -- did they ever say what it was that they were looking for? Did you ever get any information about what they -- they were looking for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Weapons and other uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they find anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No, they didn't, because we did not have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it they left and (redacted) continued to stay at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes, they left. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, thank you for telling us about that visit. Now, after that visit, were there any more visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Only when he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you about that one. So focus your mind on that day, and we'll start getting you to tell us the story about that day. Okay? Now, first of all, can you remember the date of the day that (redacted) disappeared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: It was the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who came to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Three persons; two that had been two days earlier and another one whom we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the result is that of the three people who came to your house, you didn't know the name of any of those three.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No, we didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell the Trial Chamber in your own words what happened on the day that they came.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: That day - it was around 11.00 - (redacted) was sleeping, because he had just taken his medicine. The three men came and asked for him and said that they had an order from the commander to take (redacted) for 20 minutes and he would be brought back again. Then I went and woke (redacted) up. I told him everything what I had been told, and they stayed for about ten minutes there with us. They were waiting. We didn't know them at all, because they were unknown to us. (redacted) got up and went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember how these men were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Two of them in black clothes, while the third one had a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you -- if you can recall, can you tell us if they were armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were they traveling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: They came by car, but when they came into the yard, they were on foot, of course, and they spoke to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Did you -- were you provided with any information about where they were taking him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. They said that they had an order from a commander. They didn't say where, though. They just said that they would bring him back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And these men, were they Albanians or Albanian-speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were speaking Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- did (redacted) return that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in the -- in the day or days following, did you or members of your family start to try and make inquiries about where he was and what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. We went to make inquiries. We asked in the village. There was a -- what we called a headquarters in the village in a basement. We didn't know about it, as a matter of fact, but by asking people we learned about it, and we asked, "Where is he? Why did he not come back?" And we were told, "He will be back. He will come back. Don't worry."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. In order to understand completely, the time, was it 11.00 in the morning or 11.00 in the evening when they came and took (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these inquiries, were they made in your -- in your own village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it who was telling you, "He will be back. He will come back. Don't worry"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: There were many people there. We didn't know who we were talking to. I was with my grandmother and younger brother. We went there to ask about the whereabouts of (redacted). And they just told us, "He will be back." I had the impression they didn't know what to tell us themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these men who were saying these things to you, that -- that he would be back, were they -- can you tell us how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: They were wearing everyday clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this place called a headquarters in the village, headquarters of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Headquarters of what? This was the basement of a villager.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you -- you -- you yourself, your own words are that "there was a headquarters in the village." Now, headquarters of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times did you go to the KLA headquarters making inquiries about (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Two or three times, but in vain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the only place that you were able to make inquiries, or did you go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: We only went there because we did not know where else to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us (redacted) disappeared on the -- or, sorry, the last time you saw him was on the 1st of August, 1998. Using that date as a reference point, how long did you remain in your village living in your house following that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, about a month after that we continued to stay there, because the villagers had not left yet. We were waiting for (redacted) to come back. Two or three days later a couple of people came for his medicine, and we gave them his medicine and also a jacket. But as I said, everything was in vain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know who these -- do you know the names of these people who came to collect his medicine and his jacket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen them in your village before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: No. They were not from our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if -- how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: They were wearing a green -- greenish uniform, multicoloured, I think. It was mixed colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any insignia that you could see on this uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Of the KLA on their caps and on the sleeve of their jackets. MR. DI FAZIO: Could Your Honours just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you for answering my questions, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 52, you will now be examined by Defence counsel. The first one is Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is, but I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no questions. Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where I said that you would be examined by Defence counsel, Witness 52, I did not know yet that they had no questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the following question for you: You told us about these several occasions where men came to your house first to obtain a weapon; then there was a search; and then finally, men came and (redacted) joined them and left. Now, did you at any later stage ever learn the names of any of these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt from (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what (redacted) told you about whom when that person visited you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: On the last day, when I accompanied (redacted) up to the car, we didn't know those persons that day. And (redacted) was trying to calm us down, and he said, "Don't be scared, because this is X person," and he told me the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us that name, or would you prefer to do that in private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/52
utterances.text: In private session, please, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness 52, you've answered the question put to you by Mr. Di Fazio and the question put to you by the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to testify, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, before the witness leaves the courtroom, the curtains should be pulled down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The curtains can be pulled up again. Yes. The Chamber is -- the legal officer of the Chamber, Mr. Zahar, received copies of some correspondence between the parties about disclosure issues in relation to the next witness to -- to be called. The parties also indicated that they'd like to raise the issue in court. What I see from this correspondence is that already quite some time ago in relation to the expected testimony of the witness then still on the list, Mr. Delic, that the Defence has asked -- has put six questions, questions relating to documents, questions relating to -- no, that comes later -- that you ask for whether any investigations were made in relation to, let's say, the circles, same circles as where Mr. Delic appeared as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In essence, on the 10th of May, the request to the Prosecution came in two forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There was one letter concerned with specific matters of disclosure, which has not been brought to the Trial Chamber's attention because there's no issue outstanding in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But there was also a letter drawing attention to the fact that during the Milosevic trial the position taken by the Office of the Prosecutor was that Colonel Delic, as he then was, was responsible for the commission of systematic war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Including within the indictment region, including within the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which we find in the correspondence as having been committed in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so. As well as having been involved, so it was put to him, at least in a supervisory capacity, in the disinterment and transfer for the purposes of concealment of the remains of victims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- of crimes committed by Serb forces. And in essence, what we were seeking from the Prosecution at that stage - and it's quite right to say "at that stage." It was on the assumption that he was to be a witness for the Prosecution - was clarification the Prosecution maintained those allegations; if so, whether or not they had been investigated; and if not, why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The next development -- and I -- was the Prosecution's decision to abandon Mr. Delic as a witness and thereby, in Mr. Re's view, rendering those questions moot; and his substitution by the witness who is now to be called without protective measures, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Branko Gajic. Mr. Gajic's testimony concerns matters relating to the deployment and activity of the 549th Brigade, even though he was not himself a member of that brigade and it's not been alleged by the Prosecution in past trials that he was personally involved or authorised the sorts of crimes that were alleged by the Prosecution against Colonel Delic. In essence, there were two essential issues outstanding, disclosure having been given of a number of documents and other materials. The first was a request to the Prosecution for an explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- for the decision to abandon General Delic; and the second is the outstanding request for clarification as to whether the Prosecution approaches this trial on the same basis as it approached the trial of Milosevic; namely, that General Delic and those under his command committed war crimes systematically in the indictment region during the indictment period and thereafter. Now, as far as the first matter is concerned, Mr. Re's response is contained in the letter of the 17th of October, indicating in essence that the Prosecution's decision to abandon General Delic is a non-reviewable discretion and that there's nothing to be disclosed in relation to the reasons for that decision; and in the letter of the 19th of October, as regards the second matter, in essence the Prosecution's position is that since they have taken the decision not to call General Delic, the issues of substance are moot. In short, whether the first question requires an answer or not is perhaps much less important than whether the second question requires an answer. It isn't simply a matter relevant to the credibility of the witness now abandoned. It is also a matter relevant to the conduct and the deployment of the Serb forces within the indictment region, within the indictment period and thereafter. The potential that that has for alternative explanations for otherwise unexplained deaths and for the removal and manipulation of remains. And so we would respectfully invite the Prosecution or invite the Chamber to request the Prosecution to state what its position is in relation to the conduct of the 549th under the command of General Delic, or Colonel Delic, as he then was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, that's the question that is put to you. By the way, I suggest to the parties that this whole correspondence will be perhaps in a joint filing be put on the record, because it -- it's not just a practical matter and in line with the policy that the Chamber has set out earlier, that is, either purely practical matters just by e-mail, matters of some substance to be mentioned in court, matters of greater substance to be filed. The Chamber suggests that, to have everything clearly on the record, that this correspondence will be subject to a filing. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what I'm supposed to be responding to. I mean, the Prosecution's view is we're quite mystified by the Defence pursuing a line of inquiry in relation to a witness who we advised the Trial Chamber and the Defence on the 20th of June, that is, close on four months ago, to -- to -- it's more than four months ago that we were not calling the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Emmerson is not putting the position correctly when he says the Prosecution suggested in effect, to use his phrase, in terms that General Delic was a war criminal, because we certainly didn't. Some suggestions were put to Colonel Delic as to the state of his knowledge during operations in 1998 and 1999, but the Prosecution has not taken or maintained a view in relation to Bozidar Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Branko Gajic has nothing to do with Delic. Gajic was in military intelligence in Belgrade. He was not in the 549th Brigade. As far as -- and I -- and I -- we have no knowledge that the Defence is about to put any allegations to General -- retired General Gajic, and as far as I know, Mr. Emmerson has told me they're not. The matter is not just moot. It's irrelevant. We decided not to call Delic some months ago, four months ago. We've moved on. It's just beating a dead horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether the horse is yet dead or still alive is still to be seen. Mr. Re, the way in which I understand it is the following: That the Defence would very much like to know whether the position taken by the Prosecution in the Milosevic case is that a series of crimes are committed and there was concealment of victims of crimes apart from whether Mr. Delic committed them or had some responsibility, because they may have been committed under his command, but these questions they'd like to know what the present position of the Prosecution is, because I take it that the Defence, as they said, would consider in those circumstances that there might be an alternative explanation for bodily remains being found in that area; and therefore, the Defence would like to know whether that is or still is the position of the Prosecution that crimes were committed by other forces at that time in the area so as to -- well, to see whether there's disagreement about that element between Prosecution and Defence. Mr. Emmerson, Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Harvey, is that approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's an entirely fair summary. Two matters, just if I may. First of all, I don't recall having indicated to Mr. Re that I did not wish to explore with this witness allegations of war crimes committed by Serb forces, and I certainly do. And secondly, I am slightly surprised by the suggestion that it was not the Prosecution's case in the Milosevic trial that Mr. Delic was responsible for war crimes. We've set out in our letter specific extracts from the allegations put in terms to him by counsel for the Office of the Prosecutor. For example, at paragraph 3: "The reality is that you and the police were engaged in an unrecorded exercise in ethnic cleansing. The army and the police were engaged in criminal conduct to their certain knowledge in 1998 and 1999." And paragraph 4 that: "The grave removal exercise must have been done with your knowledge and consent." It's surprising to hear Mr. Re in those circumstances suggest that that is not a fair summary or it was not fairly summarised in the way in which the matter has been put. And indeed it rather reflects the difficulty of a Prosecution position which -- which lacks clarity in respect of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I mean, that's just getting worse. Mr. Emmerson told me he wasn't going to cross-examine Mr. Gajic on crimes having been committed by Mr. Gajic. I understand that's the Defence position. In relation to whether Serbian military units committed crimes in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, well, of course they did. One only has to read the Milutinovic and Milosevic indictments to see that's the Prosecution case. There's absolutely no tension between the Prosecution prosecuting the KLA for crimes committed in 1998 and alleging that the Serbian military also committed crimes in the same -- in the -- in the same year in the same territory. In relation to whether or not there was -- whether the allegation of the Serbs taking bodies to -- from Kosovo to -- to Serbia is in somehow way connected with the allegation, which I think but cannot be sure is being made, because it hasn't been properly put to any witnesses that there was some sort of body-burying operation by the Serbs somehow in September 1998, there's no connection at all. There is nothing in the Milosevic transcript, the Milutinovic transcript, or anything in the Prosecution's possession to suggest that the Serbs planted the bodies by the canal in Lake Radonjic in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If that's what he's getting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- therefore, then, what I understand is that there is no disagreement about Serbs having committed in general terms serious crimes in the area during the time also relevant for the indictment but that the main disagreement lies in whether this could ever be an alternative or an alternative explanation for what is charged against the accused in this case. That's how I now understand the position of the Prosecution to be and where it differs from the Defence position and where it does not differ from the Defence position. I further understood that the all-relevant material is, as always, disclosed in the electronic -- in the electronic system and that from whatever the Prosecution has investigated or learned about matters in relation to the witness Delic, who's not on the list any more, or any other witness, if it would amount to Article 68 material, that would be that it could be understood to be exculpatory or may be exculpatory, which means that you might have different views on whether it exculpates or does not exculpate - that's exactly what we are just talking about that is, whether it provides for an alternative explanation for events or whether it does not. That's, of course, the interpretation and the evaluation of the material - that all disclosure obligations have been fully met by the Prosecution. Is that correctly understood, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as I know, we have disclosed all relevant material. But just one other tiny little thing, and that is the references Mr. Emmerson keeps bringing up in the Milosevic transcript. I'm sorry to say this, but he's taking them out of context. The Prosecution did not allege any specific crimes by Colonel Delic. If they had -- if we had, Mr. Emmerson would have quoted them instead of talking in terms or in summary or in paraphrasing. The -- what was suggested to Delic was he must have known something was happening. There was no specific allegation of criminality leveled against Delic, as far as I can see, and in talking to the lawyers who were in court conducting that cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand that in you're in a command position, if you know about crimes, if you haven't done anything to prevent them or to punish them, that might amount to criminal responsibility for crimes you have not committed yourself. If that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't, if I may say so, think this is the right moment for know enter a debate on this, but the Prosecution called testimony of crimes allegedly committed on the direct orders of General Delic in the Milosevic trial. Indeed, I'm going to raise some of that in cross-examination, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might too, just to make sure that we all are operating on the same basis. Since you have indicated that it's your understanding that all material has been made available to us in the electronic system, if the Court is relying on that being the electronic disclosure system, as opposed to the Prosecution identifying for the Defence what precise information is either relevant or exculpatory, which not -- has not necessarily been done with regard to -- to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be clear that any exculpatory evidence should be pointed at precisely, not to be hidden somewhere in an electronic disclosure system. That may be clear. I do understand that to the extent the Prosecution itself sees that there is material that could be considered relevant but on which it will not rely, that it nevertheless will be disclosed as relevant material in the electronic disclosure system; whereas, if the Prosecution finds anything which may be interpreted as, well, we know the exact -- just call it briefly exculpatory material, that is, material that tends to demonstrate the innocence of -- well, we have the nice formula which doesn't come literally to my mind at this moment. But under those circumstances, then specifically that attention will be labeled as potential exculpatory material and be brought to the attention of the Defence. That's how I understand the disclosure obligations, Mr. Re. And I also understand that in this respect, the Prosecution takes the position that it has met all its disclosure obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I raise a concern with that and specifically with the guidance that is found in the Karemera decision concerning the electronic disclosure system of the 30th of June, 2006, paragraph 10, in which there is specific reference to the Prosecution's duty with regard to the disclosure of information. I actually would like to note on a separate point and alert the Chamber to something which I think it probably knows from a review of the annexes, that many of the annexes that are being relied upon by the Prosecution for the testimony of the next witness happen to be authored by the very individual, Mr. Delic, who is the subject matter of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. We'll have a look at that. But then it comes more to specific documents to be used during the testimony of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The concern being, of course, that if we're in a situation where there's picking and choosing as between documents, it raises some of the problems that Mr. Emmerson raised initially and some of the difficulties that we have expressed previously with regard to whether or not the Prosecution is taking disparate positions, depending on who they are prosecuting, with regard to the evidence they're presenting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We're back -- we're back into the ballet situation of the Prosecution being splayed once again potential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is an unattractive position. Mr. Harvey, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, I fully endorse everything that has been said by my colleagues on this matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Then there was another matter and then we'll have a break. There was another matter about recently discovered material which you were seeking to add to the 65 ter list, exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's -- I think it was six reports of the 14th, a counter-intelligence brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought there were eight -- I thought there were eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's seven, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe there's -- there's seven. There's seven and a diagram. And as a result of -- of the assertions made by the Prosecution with regard to the discovery of this material, there certainly is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean -- what do you mean "assertions"? I've just made a submission as an officer of the court. I don't like being told that they're assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the facts, Mr. Re has pointed to that in support --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm agreeing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of his application, that in view of that that you do not oppose. I take it, Mr. Re, that if there would be serious doubts about the facts you would have presented, that the Defence might not have accepted your proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly don't mean to ruffle his feathers at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the position of you as well, Mr. Emmerson, and of you, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think -- unless I misunderstood the position, there was one further document produced this morning for which Mr. Re indicated that an oral application was going to be made in addition to the written application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I may have missed that. I'm thinking about the documents of which Mr. Re explained when he found them and where, not in Kosovo but in Belgrade, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. They're from the archive of the 14th Intelligence Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution didn't even know existed until the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that has been explained --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson points that there would be one other document. I'm not quite sure they know what document Mr. Emmerson is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it arrived by e-mail this morning. It's an 18th of May proclamation concerning the extending of the border belt within which the VJ constitutionally was permitted to operate to 5 kilometres. And it was served upon us as an additional document today with an indication that Mr. Re would be making an oral application to add it to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that new apart from the -- the 14th - what was it? - the 14th Intelligence Group? Is this a document that is related in any way to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, this isn't new. This was disclosed to the Defence in April 2006. It's simply a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it on the list? I think that's issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It wasn't on the list. It only came up after Mr. Zivanovic gave evidence last week about the border zones, cross-examined about the proclamation of the border zones and when it came into effect. And we found the proclamation of General -- of Colonel Lazarevic dated the 18th of May, 1998, extending the border zone 5 kilometres, referable to the Federal Republic of Yugoslav government decision of the 23rd of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, as a matter of fact, that is now raised because it gains some relevance in relation to the testimony given by Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's why we went looking for it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I certainly would have no objection to its being added. I simply note that maybe Mr. Re can clarify the position. I had thought that in re-examination with Colonel Zivanovic, Mr. Re had sought to establish that the day for the extension was the 8th of May. I don't think it was this document that was put in re-examination, but I may be wrong about that. But we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you sort that out during the break. Because if there's no objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, now clarifications could be sought during the break. May I take it, Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey, that since you are not jumping up that you would agree with the -- with the other documents about the 14th Intelligence - what was it? - Group, that there's no objection against adding them to the 65 ter list? In the absence --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've already indicated that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was looking at Mr. Harvey. Okay. Then that request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the exhibits, could it be -- could they be done in the same way as we did Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Stijovic, that is, they be given numbers by the registrar in the spreadsheet so that they can sequentially follow with this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would that be a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think there are 35 -- 37 annexes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, Mr. Registrar asks me whether it's your intention to have them MFI'd first or whether it -- this is already an announcement of tendering them. I take it that that only comes during the testimony. So just first to give them numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's an announcement of an intention to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But first get an MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll take it in two steps. Then since we have to change from interpreter teams, we need a break of half an hour. We will resume and -- at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the oral submissions by the parties and the order to file the correspondence is still there, but it -- the Chamber finds no reason the exchange of views until now not to start with the witness at this moment. I have another request for you. I asked -- and I said similarly and earlier was talked about this week to receive a response on the videolink. If there would be a possibility, even if by oral submissions, to express yourself at an earlier stage, the videolink has been scheduled for the 31st of October. It needs quite a lot of time to prepare for it. So if that would be possible already by tomorrow, that would be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We will meet after court or during one of the sessions and try to get back to the Chamber as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Your cooperation is much appreciated. Then, finally, my attention was drawn to the fact that there might be some unclarity as to the eight documents to be added on the 65 ter list. I think I said at one moment that the request was granted. If I have not said that, then I hereby say that the addition to the 65 ter list of the eight documents is granted. And I noticed that there were no objections against the other document, which you have sorted out over the break, Mr. Emmerson, with Mr. Re, I take it? Or at least there's -- there's no major problem there. So therefore no problems with that respect. Neither. Then, Mr. Gajic, it's very unpolite not to address a witness who appears in court and to deal with other procedural matters. Apologies for that. Mr. Gajic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Re, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Your name is Branko Gajic. Your date of birth is the 17th of July, 1944. And you are a retired major general from the Serbian army and before that, the VJ and the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you recently testified in the case Milutinovic, et cetera. So you're familiar with these proceedings and the process here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you a statement which you have a copy there in hard copy, dated the 2nd of October, 2007. It's of some 18 pages in English. It's a statement I wish to tender under Rule 92 ter of the Rules of Procedure. But first I have to ask you two questions. I note that no objection has been made to any portion of this statement to this point. The first one is: Does it bear your declaration and is true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the second question is: If I were to ask you the questions to which answers are given in this statement, would you give that same testimony in this court?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it's 65 ter number 2090. May it be received into evidence on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I think the first question is not whether it was signed by the witness but whether he has read the statement and whether this statement reflects the answers you gave at the time. Is that the reason why you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, since there are no objections, then, Mr. Registrar, the exhibit number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P1138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Since there are no objections, it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in front of you, Mr. Gajic, do you have a folder there containing the 38 documents which you have referred to in your statement including your diagram which is the first annex? Just to confirm that you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just reading the transcript, I missed the word "and is true" otherwise, I would not have added that question. I refer to page 50, line 24. It says: "Does it bear your declaration and is true?" I understood whether he has signed it. But if I would have read this, I would not have added the question I put to the witness before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm always confused by the wording of 92 ter myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not confused. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going ask you some questions about the statement to clarify some of the things in your statement to give the Trial Chamber a better picture of the contents of your statement. The first thing I'm going to ask you about is the 29 -- in paragraph 1, you refer to having had 29 years in the counter-intelligence service of the military in which you served and your retirement position was, I understand, as the deputy head of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Assistant and deputy at the same time. This is how it was officially proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In terms of seniority, where were you in the military hierarchy as of your retirement on the 31st of December, 2001, as a major-general?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: In early October 2000, I, together with General Vasiljevic, who was deputy head of the administration, removed -- was removed from that position and other people were brought in. I was appointed to a different sector, to an additional formation. However, pursuant to the order of the then-Chief of the General Staff, I and General Vasiljevic was reassigned to the security administration and worked there until our retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: General, please focus on the question, if you can. And the question was: Where were you in the terms of the military hierarchy as of the date of your retirement? Number one, two, three, four, five, six, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the security administration, I was number three there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1998, in the period covered by the indictment, what was your level of seniority?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I was both number two and number three. I was deputy head of the administration and assistant to the head of the administration, which means man number two and man number three.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's in the security administration.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about in the military? Could you rank where you were in the military hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The security administration is one of the independent administrations of the General Staff, and the head of the security administration is one of the assistants to the Chief of the General Staff. In his absence, I stepped in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you were fairly senior in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there military secrets to which you would not have had access in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Whatever came within the competence of the military security was known to me. There were no secrets in that domain that I was not aware of. And even broadly speaking, in relation to military matters, to the matters of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to turn to paragraph 6 of your statement. If that could just be displayed in English in Sanction and if you could look at the hard copy in front of you, please. That's the paragraph where you refer to: "Counter-intelligence reports being distinct from other types of routine reporting in the VJ; namely, operational reporting and command reporting." And then you say: "Counter-intelligence reports would often contain information from operations reports, to the extent that it was relevant to the mandate of the UB." The next paragraph, which is 7, you refer to an independent unit in Kosovo called the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group. What was the role of the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group within the VJ in that time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The 14th Counter-Intelligence Group, as you say - and it is mentioned here - was connected to the security administration and it was the spatial structure, the territorial structure of the counter-intelligence service covering the situation on the ground with regard to the activities placing the army and the defence system in jeopardy, and it went down from the service to the unit commands, and it directly reported to the security administration on its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You say in that statement that it had about 20 individuals. Where did they work from? Where were they based?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: They were based in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they do fieldwork?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Trial Chamber how they went about their fieldwork, that is, how they collected their information in the field.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: They had, as we called it, their intelligence sources in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and these intelligence sources were members of the population, civilians, as well as members of different army structures residing in the area. Furthermore, they exchanged information with the MUP and the State Security Service and had daily contacts with the population which were quite well-developed. The population was not -- were not agents as such, but they were informants on whom they relied. And these were the ways on the basis of which they gathered information. And I apologise, they also exchanged intelligence with military intelligence organs, because they also had their infrastructure in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I want to ask you about informants. You just referred to "informants upon whom they relied." What was the difference between the type of informants the DB was using and the type of informants that military intelligence was using?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: There was no difference, except for the fact that this was the counter-intelligence department, as it is written here, and the difference lay in the contents of the information that was of interest. The counter-intelligence service was interested in the information concerning whatever placed the army in jeopardy; whereas, the military -- or rather, the State Security Service was interested in the situation in general, including that which concerned the army itself. The sources were more or less the same and the methodology they used was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did counter-intelligence have informants within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say in 1998 approximately how many informants were within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you with any precision. Still there were sufficient numbers of them, because some of the sources were developed in early 1980s and are still being used to this day. Therefore, I can't tell you how many there were. The 14th Department certainly had no less than 50 or 60 different sources of different ranking, quality, and so on and so forth, and I'm only referring to the counter-intelligence department and not referring to the counter-intelligence structures of the different units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 50 or 60 different sources, were they within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: There were those among them who were in the KLA and others who had direct or indirect contacts or links with the KLA. For instance, some of them had close relatives or friends who were members of the KLA, and these were what we call indirect contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said they were of different ranking and quality. First I'm going to ask you about the ranking, then quality. How high up within the KLA - and no names, of course - were these sources placed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part they were former officers of the Yugoslav People's Army with whom operative contacts were made in 1981 and later, at the time of those mass-scale demonstrations you're probably aware of, and we had actions combatting such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just concentrate on 1998 for the moment. In 1998, how high up within the KLA were informants for counter-intelligence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact figure now or the exact information. There were those among them who held the rank of major, even lieutenant colonel, and then the occasional colonel as well of the former JNA. I don't know which ranks they held in the KLA. I know the duties they held. They were commanders, chiefs of staffs, and so on and so forth. And, of course, I'm aware of the ranks they held in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also said they were of different quality. How did your department assess the quality of the information it was receiving from these informants? In other words, what was the methodology used to assess its reliability and quality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The main practice was vetting. Or rather, we double-checked the information that they provided us with against other sources. Secondly, we would have some earlier information about the activities or events they were supposed to gather information on. So we would double-check that with the MUP, with the security service, with the intelligence service, and we did that. If the persons involved had for many years had operative contacts with the intelligence service, we already had some valid indicators of their sincerity, veracity, reliability, and so on and so forth, but we always double-checked the information we received from them, especially if the information was sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to take you to an example of a report. It's annex 3 of your statement -- of the -- the bundle there. It's dated the 23rd of January, 1998. If that could be displayed in e-court, please. If you could just go to annex 3. It's the report of Colonel -- Chief Colonel Aco Tomic, 23rd of January, 1998 to the VJ -- I think it's GS -- General Staff of the VJ Security Service, 3rd Army. That's -- and it -- it says: "Through operative work by the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group and the Pristina Corps, information was obtained regarding an armed clash on the territory of the Srbica-Donje Prekaze village, kidnapping and maltreatment of Serbs by members of the so-called KLA, the presence of members of the 'Serbian Guard', headed by Arkan, and propaganda by the Albanian media in the state and abroad." And then it refers to the attack on the Jashari compound, and then it goes down to refer to three other particular incidents. The ones I wish to ask you about are on the 22nd of April, 1998, there's an attack on Desko Vasic, an assemblyman in the Zvecan Municipal Assembly --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: 22nd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I meant January.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, whilst there is that interruption, lest the transcript should remain unclear, the reference is not to the attack on the Jashari compound in the sense that we have heard other evidence about the attack in March but to earlier incident in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, quite. There's one on the 22nd of January, 1998, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are three particular incidents described which I ask you to comment on. That's 22nd of January, 1998; the attack on Desko Vasic, the stopping of a bus on the same day on the Klina-Srbica road by the so-called KLA inflicting serious bodily injuries on Nenad Nikolic; and thirdly, the stopping by a KLA patrol of Ljiljana Ilijev, a public -- or employee of the SDK public auditing service and her sister Darinka Andjelkovic. The two of them were maltreated and then released with the words "your brothers are killing our brothers." What I want you to comment on and tell the Trial Chamber is the source of those three incidents allowing it to come into this particular report by Chief Colonel Aco Tomic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The first incident, which took place on the 22nd of January, 1998, relating to Desko Vasic, who was a deputy of the Zvecan Assembly, Municipal Assembly, was reported by his relatives, because the man went to work and never showed up. And then on the 23rd, when the MUP - because this was within the competence of the MUP - tried to conduct an investigation, he was found killed next to his car with another passenger, who was unidentified at the time. That's the first incident. The second incident also had to do with the stopping of the bus on the Klina-Srbica road, where the bus was pulled over. The IDs were asked of the passengers, who were maltreated and beaten up. The information was received from the driver and the other passengers who reported the incident and described the perpetrators. As a result of that, since the perpetrators wore uniforms with the KLA insignia, it was concluded that they were indeed responsible for this. And then the third incident, which also took place on the 22nd of January, 1998, involving this lady Ljiljana and her sister, she reported the incident to the MUP. She described the problems she had and she told them what she had observed, the trench-digging and so on and so forth. And also on the basis of the -- or rather, it was on the basis of -- of our regular exchanges of information with the MUP that we received the information. And the head of the 14th Counter-Intelligence Department thought it interesting enough to be sent to the security administration and the command of the 3rd army and to report to them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why were incidents of this nature being included in intelligence -- or counter-intelligence reports going up through the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: They were significant because we followed what was happening in the area to the civilian population. The strategy of the leadership of the secessionist movement was to carry out ethnic cleansing, not only of Serbs, Montenegrins, but also of many, many Albanians who were deemed loyal to the Serbian state, were styled as spies. They suffered a great deal. They were targeted. And we were monitoring the situation and the developments with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I appreciate the question did not set out to elicit inadmissible opinion evidence of that nature, but I wonder if Mr. Re might confine the witness or control the answers in a way that doesn't allow them to transgress into areas which are not proper for the witness to be giving opinion evidence about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we come to the next part of the report -- Of course, I will endeavour to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's implicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next part. Underneath that, you refer to -- sorry, it refers to "operative information" indicated that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, is on the territory of Zvecan municipality with members of the Serbian Guard. They are staying in the Trojka Hotel.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Zvecan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise for my sloppy pronunciation. The next paragraph: "This stay was noted a few days ago when Arkan came to this area by helicopter." What the significance of that particular incident, that is, Arkan's presence there, such that it was put in this report? I mean, why was the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group reporting on Arkan's presence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Because the unit of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was in view of the army a paramilitary formation. They were in contacts with the State Security Service but in the army's view, they were a paramilitary formation. There existed a strict order of the Chief of Staff according to which paramilitary forces and groups should not be allowed access in Kosovo and Metohija. Therefore, they arrived there without the approval or the knowledge of the army and it was considered that this ought to be included in the report. Besides, there were great problems precisely with that formation -- there had been great problems with that formation ever since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
